paragraphs: §1 — The soul persists by God's power after the body; why reward and punishment do not come immediately upon death

We said, at the end of the seventh bab, that the spirits, after their separation from the bodies, may be in a requital of the kind of the spiritual requital (jazāʾ min jins al-jazāʾ al-rūḥānī) until they are raised a second time in their bodies — since it is not admissible that they remain neglected (muhmala), having no portion of the fruits of their deeds and their deserts (istiḥqāqāt). And since it has been established, by what has already been mentioned, that [the soul] persists after the bodies, there yet remains for us, in this discourse, something we did not exhaust there which we need to mention here — namely the saying of one who asks, saying: how is it admissible that the soul subsist by itself after its separation from the body? The answer to that is that God sustains it by His power.

: The bab opens by retrieving the thesis left at the end of Bab 7 (cited as "the seventh bab"): the soul persists after death in an interim jazāʾ rūḥānī (requital of a spiritual kind) until the bodily resurrection treated in Bab 8. The premise — that the soul cannot be left muhmala (neglected, idle, without the fruits of its deserts) — is the eschatological-justice axiom of the whole thawāb / ʿiqāq block (glossary §VI: istiḥqāq, thawāb, ʿiqāb). The "how can a soul subsist without a body?" question is answered minimally here (by divine power) and developed at length in §§11-12.
§2 — God assigned distinct abodes and times: this world for obligation, a separate abode for requital

As for the reason that the reward and the punishment do not come immediately upon the soul's separation from the body — it is that the Creator (sublime be His praise) made for the creation ranks and bounds that do not enter one into another. He made this abode the abode of obligation and of work (dār al-taklīf wa-l-ʿamal) and set for it a bound and a terminus; and likewise He made for the requital another abode, and set for it a [certain] bound and a known time. So just as it is not admissible that, in the time of requital alone, there be work or obligation, likewise it is not admissible that, in the time of obligation, there be neither reward nor punishment — I mean the complete, unmixed reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-tāmm al-ṣarf). And it was necessary that there be for that another abode, other than the abode of work, in which all those to be requited — the rewarded and the punished — are gathered, and in which they are requited. And if a questioner asks about the time of the Messiah and his days, which of the two abodes that is, we shall say [the answer] concerning that at the end of the Maqala.

: The structural heart of the bab: the Creator has laid out marātib wa-ḥudūd (ranks and bounds) that "do not enter one into another," so that the present world is exclusively the dār al-taklīf wa-l-ʿamal (the abode of obligation and works) and requital belongs to a wholly separate abode and time. The qualifier al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-tāmm al-ṣarf ("the complete, unmixed recompense") is what is deferred — leaving room for the interim spiritual requital of §1, §13. The deferral of the Messianic-age question "to the end of the Maqala" is one of Q's recurring forward cross-references (cf. Bab 6 §§3, 9, 12).
§3 — The objection: the saints shunned death — Hezekiah's weeping

Then we return and say: perhaps an objector will object to this statement and say: if this were as you have said, the saints (al-awliyāʾ) would not abhor death — rather they would seek it and long for it; yet we have seen a number of them abhor it and beg to be spared it. That is, for instance, חזקיהו (Hezekiah, peace be upon him), who, when the prophet (peace be upon him) informed him of [his] death, found it grievous and wept a great weeping, since he says [Isa 38:10] אני אמרתי בדמי ימי אלכה בשערי שאול פקדתי יתר שנותי ("I said: in the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of Sheol, I am deprived of the remainder of my years") — and he calls [the remainder of his years] "twenty," bearing witness in Hebrew; [Isa 38:3] ויבך יחזקיהו בכי גדול ("and Hezekiah wept a great weeping"). Now, had he known that that to which he passes through death is better than the life of this world, he would not have abhorred the better and desired the inferior.

: The objection that drives §§3-10: if the soul's post-mortem state is good, why did the saints dread death? The lead case is Hezekiah (Isa 38:10, 38:3), who wept at Isaiah's death-sentence. The opaque phrase wa-shahida bi-ʿibrānī ʿishrīn ("and he bears witness in Hebrew [to] twenty") is Q's gloss connecting Hezekiah's "remainder of my years" to the fifteen years added in Isa 38:5 — read here, with the prior allotment, as a span he reckoned at "twenty"; the syntax is compressed and the figure is left as Q gives it. The objection is sharpened in §3-end by the principle "no one abhors the better and desires the inferior."
§3 (continued) — David's many laments against death; only those in extremity sought it

And likewise we have seen דאוד (David, peace be upon him) censure death in more than one place, and abhor it, and beg to be spared it, when he says [Ps 118:17] לא אמות כי אחיה וגו' ("I shall not die but live") — and this is not a report but a request and a longing — and he says after it [Ps 118:18] יסר יסרני יה ולמות לא נתנני ("the Lord has chastened me sorely, but He has not given me over to death"); and he says also [Ps 88:12] כי לא תעצב נפשי לשאול ("for my soul shall not be grieved unto Sheol"); and he says [Ps 6:5] שובה ה' חלצה נפשי וגו' ("return, O Lord, deliver my soul") — meaning, from death, since he says after it [Ps 6:6] כי אין במות זכרך וגו' ("for in death there is no remembrance of You"); and he says [Ps 102:25] אֹמַר אֵלִי אַל תַּעֲלֵנִי בַּחֲצִי יָמָי בְּדוֹר דורים וגו' ("I say: O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days, [You] whose years are throughout all generations"); and he says [Ps 116:8] חי חלצת נפשי ממות וגו' ("[You] have delivered my soul from death"); and he says [Ps 33:18] הנה עין יי אל יראיו וגו' להציל ממות נפשם וגו' ("behold, the eye of the Lord is upon those who fear Him … to deliver their soul from death"); and also [Ps 30:10] מה בצע בְּדָמִי בְּרִדְתִּי אֶל שַׁחַת וגו' ("what profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit?"); and also [Ps 116:15] יָקָר בְּעֵינֵי יי הַמָּוְתָה לַחֲסִידָיו ("precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones").

And we have seen no one long for death or seek it save one who was in extremity (shidda) — that is, for instance, Jonah, of whom it is said [Jonah 4:8] וישאל את נפשו למות ("and he asked that his soul might die"), and that was on account of what befell him of the severity of the pain of the sun's heat and the harshness of its torment; and likewise אליהו (Elijah, peace be upon him), in his saying [1 Kgs 19:4] ויאמר רב עתה יי קח נפשי ("and he said: it is enough; now, O Lord, take my soul"), and that too was for a cause — what he was in of the fear of the killing with which איזבל (Jezebel) was threatening him; and the like of that, Job, in his saying [Job 3:11] למא לא מרחם אמות וגו' ("why did I not die from the womb?"), and that was on account of the marvels that befell him — the loss of property and children and the pains that followed in his body; and likewise ירמיהו (Jeremiah), in his saying [Job 3:10] אשר לא מותתני מרחם וגו' ("[because] He did not slay me from the womb"), [Jer 20:18] למה זה מרחם יצאתי וגו' ("why did I come forth from the womb?"); and Job too has explained that, in his saying [Job 3:20] למה יתן לעמל אור וחיים למרי נפש המחכים למות ואיננו וגו' ("why is light given to him in misery, and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death, but it comes not?").

: A dense scriptural catalogue of saintly recoil from death (David, Pss 118, 88, 6, 102, 116, 33, 30) capped by the counter-class — only those in extremity (shidda) sought death: Jonah (sunstroke, Jonah 4:8), Elijah (fear of Jezebel, 1 Kgs 19:4), Job (Job 3:11, 3:20), Jeremiah (Job 3:10 / Jer 20:18). The point prepares §4: that death is desired only as relief from suffering proves it is not desired as a passage to a better state. Several OCR'd references in this passage are corrupt or transposed in the underlying manuscript (the diff-report flags 257 Hebrew disagreements across the bab); the verse pointers have been silently corrected to standard versification where Q's quoted Hebrew makes the referent certain (e.g., Q's pointer "ל'" at Ps 33:18 / Ps 30:10). One attribution in the source is itself anomalous: the words quoted at "ירמיהו … [Job 3:10]" are from Job, not Jeremiah; Q (or his copyist) appears to have run Job 3:10 and Jer 20:18 together under Jeremiah's name. Left as Q gives it, flagged here.
§4 — Death is praiseworthy only in extremity; God's promise of long life to the obedient

So you do not see death praised at all, nor sought, save by the people of extremities, trials, and calamities (ahl al-shadāʾid wa-l-balwā wa-l-maṣāʾib). As for others — those who are in ease and bounty — they only abhor it and flee from it and seek its opposite, which is life. So were that to which the righteous one passes after death good and more praiseworthy, none of the righteous would flee from it nor desire its opposite, which is the lesser and the more deficient in good.

And the confirmation of that is what God (sublime be His majesty) promised, to whoever obeys, of length of life, when He says [Deut 30:20] כי הוא חייך וארך ימיך ("for He is your life and the length of your days"), and His saying [Deut 11:21] לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם וִימֵי בניכם וגו' ("that your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children"). And for this שלמה (Solomon) said in Proverbs [Prov 3:2] כי אֹרֶך ימים ושנות חיים ושלום יוסיפו לך ("for length of days and years of life and peace shall they add to you"), and he said [Prov 10:27] יראת יי תוסיף ימים ("the fear of the Lord adds days"). So were the righteous and their spirits, immediately upon death, to pass to a bliss — and that bliss more excellent than the bliss of this world — the Creator would not promise whoever obeyed with length of life in this world, and whoever disobeyed Him with its shortness.

: Q's first answer (general): death is "praiseworthy only for the people of extremity," never for those at ease — proving it is sought as relief, not as a good. He then mounts a second argument from the Torah's promise of long life to the obedient (Deut 30:20; Deut 11:21) and short life to the wicked (with Prov 3:2, 10:27): if death immediately ushered the righteous into a superior bliss, long earthly life could not be the promised reward. This sets up the puzzle §6 will resolve (why promise the lesser good of longevity at all?).
§5 — Scripture's own testimony that the righteous find rest in death

It is confirmed also by the saying of ישעיהו (Isaiah, peace be upon him) [Isa 57:1-2] כי מפני הרעה נאסף הצדיק וגו' ("the righteous is taken away from the evil to come"), and the saying of God (blessed and exalted) to ירמיהו (Jeremiah, peace be upon him) [2 Kgs 22:20] לכן הנני אֹספך אל אבותיך ("therefore, behold, I will gather you to your fathers"); and Solomon says in Qohelet [Eccl 2:17] ושנאתי את החיים כי רע עלי המעשה ("and I hated life, for the work was grievous to me"); and he says also in Proverbs [Prov 14:32] וחסה במותו צדיק וגו' ("but the righteous has refuge in his death") — and he reported that the righteous one is sheltered in his death, trusting in it, since he knows that he passes to what is more excellent than what he is in of this world; and he says also in Qohelet [Eccl 7:1] טוב שם משמן טוב ויום המות מיום הולדו ("a good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of one's birth") — meaning that the day of death is better than the day of birth for one whose name is good; and it is impossible that the day of death be better than the day of birth, except that going out from the world, for the righteous one and for him whose name is good, is better than abiding in it. And Asaph (upon him be mercy) says in Psalms [Ps 73:25] מי לי בַשָּׁמָיִם ועמך לא חפצתי בארץ וגו' ("whom have I in heaven [but You]? and with You I desire nothing on earth") — he said: who is mine, that I might be in heaven and with You, O my God? for I have no desire to be on earth. And this is most emphatic in the righteous one's preferring and choosing death — which is the return of the spirit to the Creator (mighty and exalted) and its being with Him — over abiding on earth.

But [against this] we say in answer to that: we say first that it has been established that the soul persists after the body — and that by what we have already mentioned of the saying of שלמה (Solomon) in Qohelet [Eccl 12:7] והרוח תשוב אל האלהים אשר נתנה וגו' ("and the spirit returns to God who gave it"), and the saying of אביגיל (Abigail) [1 Sam 25:29] והיתה נפש אדני צרורה בצרור החיים ("and the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life") and its completion, and the saying of שלמה in Qohelet [Eccl 3:21] ומי יודע רוח בני האדם העֹלה היא למעלה ("and who knows the spirit of the children of men, whether it goes upward?"). Then we also said, after that, that it is not admissible that the spirit be neglected. And it remained for us to derive the meanings of these passages (al-fawāsīq) and what they admit of interpretation. So we say: it has been established that the spirits of the righteous and the upright cannot, after death, pass to extremity or to pain — since some of them, those who were in extremity, had sought death and longed for it, and it is absurd that one should long and seek to be transferred from extremity to extremity and from pain to pain. So this is, beyond doubt, an indication that he sought only to be transferred from extremity and pain to rest and ease — and for this Job (peace be upon him) said [Job 3:13] כי עתה שכבתי ואשקוט ישנתי אז ינוח לי וגו' ("for now I should have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept; then had I been at rest"), and he said [Job 3:17] ושם ינוחו יגיעי כח ("there the weary in strength are at rest") — meaning those who have toiled in obedience: there shall be for them rest, and there is no bounty more delightful than rest.

: The catalogue of pro-death prooftexts the objector marshals: the righteous "gathered from before the evil" (Isa 57:1-2), Josiah "gathered to your fathers" before the disaster (2 Kgs 22:20), Qohelet's "I hated life" (Eccl 2:17) and "the day of death is better than the day of birth" (Eccl 7:1), the righteous who "has refuge in his death" (Prov 14:32), and Asaph's longing to be with God and not on earth (Ps 73:25). The objector reads these as proof that death is simply better for the righteous — the return of the spirit to the Creator and its being with Him — which (the objector infers) tells against the soul's awaiting a deferred bodily recompense. Q grants the persistence of the soul but will redirect the verses (in the continuation, n. 7) to mean rest from suffering, not a completed reward.

: §5 piles up the pro-death witnesses (the righteous "gathered from evil," Isa 57:1-2; Jeremiah "gathered to his fathers," 2 Kgs 22:20; Qohelet's "the day of death is better"; Asaph's "with You I desire nothing on earth," Ps 73:25), then pivots to the resolution: the soul does persist (Eccl 12:7; 1 Sam 25:29's tzeror ha-ḥayyim; Eccl 3:21), and the saints who sought death sought rest from suffering (Job 3:13, 3:17), not a transfer "from extremity to extremity." The term al-fawāsīq (rendered "passages") is Q's word for scriptural verses/pericopes requiring taʾwīl. The interim state is one of rest (rāḥa) for the righteous — consistent with the deferral of full recompense (§2) and the foretaste-doctrine of §13.
§6 — God's promise of long life is an accommodation to the soul's love of the immediate

As for the Creator's (mighty and exalted) promise to people of length of life, by His saying [Deut 30:20] כי הוא חייך וארך ימיך וגו' ("for He is your life and the length of your days") — completing the mention of it, Solomon's [Prov 3:2], and his [Moses'] saying [Deut 11:21] למען ירבו ימיכם וימי בניכם ("that your days and your children's days may be multiplied") — the meaning of that is that people are by nature disposed to the love of the good that is hastened (al-khayr al-muʿajjal), even if the deferred (al-ājil) is more excellent. So the Creator (exalted be He) greatly loved, in completing His promise to them, [to add,] upon the obedience [whose reward is] the abundant deferred reward, that He would join to that also a promise of an immediate bliss (naʿīm ʿājil), so that their souls might be set at rest by it, and that the proof against them might be the more binding — since there would have befallen them, for obedience, both an immediate promise and a deferred promise. And that is because the people, during the length of their stay in Egypt, were slaves in misery and toil; then they were transferred from that to a desolate wilderness; and it is the way of one who was thus that his soul should yearn toward an immediate bliss, and seek it, and incline to it. So He promised them that toward which their souls incline and which they crave, so that nothing of what they want and love should remain unattained for them.

: The resolution of the §4 puzzle: why promise longevity (the lesser, mundane good) if the deferred otherworldly reward is greater? Because the soul is maṭbūʿ (innately disposed) to love al-khayr al-muʿajjal — the immediate good — even when the ājil (deferred) good is superior. The earthly promise is thus a pedagogical accommodation to human psychology, doubly binding the proof (ḥujja) against the disobedient. The Exodus-to-wilderness illustration grounds the accommodation historically: a people fresh from slavery naturally craves immediate relief, so God's promise meets them where they are. This muʿajjal / ājil (immediate vs. deferred good) distinction will organize the four formal answers of §§7-10.
§7 — First answer: the soul's innate aversion to parting from companions

As for the saints' seeking of life and what appeared of their abhorrence of death — there are in it four answers. The first of them is what has already been mentioned, of what the souls have been by nature disposed to — the inclination to the immediate pleasure (al-ladhdha al-ʿājila); and along with that also what they have been disposed to of the abhorrence of parting from saints, protectors, kinsmen, and loved ones. So it is admissible that one of the saints who abhorred death only went, in that, along with what custom has established — what the soul has been disposed to of that — so as not to hasten parting from his saints, his loved ones, and his kinsmen. This is one aspect.

: The first formal answer recapitulates §§6-8: the saints' recoil is partly the soul's innate love of the ladhdha ʿājila (immediate pleasure of continued life) and partly its natural aversion to separation from loved ones — a "going along with custom" (mā jarat bihi al-ʿāda), not a judgment that death is bad. The answer concedes a natural (non-evaluative) dread, leaving the evaluative claim (death is worse) untouched.
§8 — Second answer: longer life means more obedience and so greater reward

The second [answer]: that the righteous one, the longer his life lasts, the more his work for obedience, and the more abundant and excellent his reward upon that. So the saints' seeking of life was for this cause — namely that they might increase in work, so that the reward be multiplied for them. And that is the like of the saying of דוד (David) [Ps 118:17] לא אמות כי אחיה ואספר מעשי יה ("I shall not die but live, and declare the works of the Lord"), and his saying [Ps 119:175] תְּחִי נפשי ותהללך וגו' ("let my soul live, and it shall praise You"), and his saying also [Ps 119:88] כְּחַסְדְּךָ חַיֵּנִי וְאֶשְׁמְרָה עֵדוּת פִּיךָ וגו' ("quicken me according to Your mercy, that I may keep the testimony of Your mouth"), and his saying [Ps 118:18] יסֹר יִסְּרַנִּי יָּהּ וְלַמָּוֶת לֹא נְתָנָנִי וגו' ("the Lord has chastened me sorely, but has not given me over to death"), and he says after it [Ps 118:19] פתחו לי שערי צדק אבוא בם אודה יה וגו' ("open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and give thanks to the Lord"). So he reported, in these sayings, that he seeks life only to thank God and praise Him, recount his deeds, and keep the ordinances — and these are all acts of obedience that necessitate the increase of the deferred reward. And the like of that also is his saying [Ps 119:17] גְּמֹל עַל עַבְדְּךָ אֶחְיֶה וגו' ("deal bountifully with Your servant, that I may live"), and he followed that with his saying

: The second answer (the most theologically loaded): the saints sought life to accrue more reward through more obedience — longer life = more ʿamal = more thawāb ājil. The Davidic prooftexts (Pss 118:17, 119:175, 119:88, 118:18-19, 119:17) are all read as petitions for life for the sake of praising God and keeping the commandments. This presupposes the istiḥqāq (desert) economy of the eschatology block: reward is proportioned to obedience, so a longer life of obedience is genuinely advantageous even granting that the deferred state is superior. §8 runs without break into §9 in the source.
§9 — Third answer: the wish to see vindication over one's enemies

[Ps 16:11] תּוֹדִיעֵנִי אֹרַח חַיִּים וגו' ("You will make known to me the path of life") — so he made known that he seeks survival and life in order to know the path of life, which is the reward that obedience necessitates, as he said [Deut 30:15] ראה נתתי לפניך היום את החיים ואת הטוב וגו' ("see, I have set before you this day life and good"); and he confirmed that by his saying [Ps 16:11] שׂבַע שמחות את פניך נעימות בימינך נצח ("fullness of joys is in Your presence, delights at Your right hand for evermore") — that is, that his aim is the satiety of the joys that are before God, and the bliss that is unto the uttermost; and that, beyond doubt, is the deferred reward. And the like of that is his saying [Ps 6:5] שׁוּבָה יְיָ חַלְּצָה נַפְשִׁי וגו' ("return, O Lord, deliver my soul"), and his saying right after it [Ps 6:6] כי אין במות זכרך בִשְׁאוֹל מִי יוֹדֶה לָּךְ ("for in death there is no remembrance of You; in Sheol who shall give You thanks?"); and for this he said [Hab 1:12] ה' לא נמות כִּי לֹא שְׁאוֹל תּוֹדֶךָּ מָוֶת יְהַלְלֶךָ וגו' חי חי הוא יודך כיום היום וגו' ("O Lord, we shall not die … for Sheol does not thank You, death does not praise You … the living, the living, he shall thank You, as I do this day"), and the saying of David also [Ps 30:10] מה בֶּצַע בְּדָמִי בְּרִדְתִּי אֶל שָׁחַת הֲיוֹדְךָ עָפָר וגו' ("what profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit? shall the dust praise You?").

The third [answer] is that [they sought life] in order that they might see the retributions upon their enemies, and that their enemies not see [retributions] upon them, so as to rejoice and gloat over them. For nothing is more wounding to the soul than the gloating of the enemy, nor more soothing to the eye of [one who has] an enemy than gloating over the enemy. And that is the like of the saying of David [Ps 35:19] אל ישמחו לי איבי שקר וגו' ("let not those who are wrongfully my enemies rejoice over me"), [Ps 35:1 / Ps 119:154] בָּרוּךְ יְיָ אֲשֶׁר רָב אֶת רִיב חֶרְפָּתִי מִיַּד נָבָל ("blessed be the Lord, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of the base"), and his saying [Ps 118:7] יי' לי בעוזרי וגו' ("the Lord is for me among my helpers"); and more emphatic than that is his saying [Ps 13:4] הָאִירָה עֵינַי פֶּן אִישַׁן המות פן יאמר אויבי יכלתיו וגו' ("lighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, 'I have prevailed against him'"); and he said [Ps 43:1] שפטני אלֹהִים וריבה ריבי וגו' ("judge me, O God, and plead my cause"), and he said also [Ps 35:24] שפטני כצדקך יי' אלהי ואל ישמחו לי ואל יאמרו בלבם האח נפשנו אל יאמרו בלענוהו וגו' ("judge me according to Your righteousness, O Lord my God, and let them not rejoice over me … let them not say, 'we have swallowed him up'"), and his saying [Ps 41:12] בְּזֹאת יָדַעְתִּי כִּי חָפַצְתָּ בִּי כִּי לֹא יָרִיעַ אויבי עָלָי ("by this I know that You delight in me, that my enemy does not triumph over me"), and he said [Ps 25:2] אל יעלצו אויבי לי וגו' ("let not my enemies exult over me"), and he said [Ps 41:3] ואל תתנהו בנפש איביו וגו' ("and do not give him up to the will of his enemies"), [Ps 27:12] אל תתנני בנפש צרי וגו' ("do not give me up to the will of my adversaries"), [Ps 58:11] ישמח צדיק כי חזה נקם וגו' ("the righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance"), [and he said] [Ps 59:11] אלהים יראני בשוררי ("God shall let me look upon my enemies"); and יחזקאל (Ezekiel) says to the king

: The third answer: the saints clung to life to witness vindication over their enemies and to deny those enemies the shamāta (malicious gloating) of outliving them. Q opens it with a heavy chain of Davidic enemy-Psalms (Pss 35, 118, 13, 43, 41, 25, 27, 58, 59). The psychological maxim — "nothing is more wounding to the soul than the enemy's gloating" — anticipates §13's claim that the soul itself (not the body) is the seat of such pleasure and pain. The Hab 1:12 quotation runs together fragments of the verse with the marginal ḥai ḥai hu yodekha (cf. Isa 38:19), as Q's source presents them; the bracketed references are reconstructed from the quoted Hebrew, several of Q's marginal pointers being corrupt in the OCR.
§10 — Fourth answer: lest God's enemies find an occasion to blaspheme

[Ezek 28:17] גָּבַהּ לִבְּךָ בְּיָפְיֶךָ וגו' ("your heart was lifted up because of your beauty") — then he says [Ezek 28:17] לִפְנֵי מְלָכִים נְתַתִּיךָ לְרַאֲוָה ("before kings I have set you, that they may gaze [upon you]"); and שלמה (Solomon) says in Proverbs [Prov 29:16] וְצַדִּיקִים בְּמַפַּלְתָּם יִרְאוּ ("and the righteous shall look upon their downfall"); and מיכה (Micah) says [Mic 7:10] וְתֵרֶא אוֹיִבְתִּי וּתְכַסֶּהָ בוּשָׁה וגו' עֵינַי תִּרְאֶינָה בָּהּ עַתָּה תִּהְיֶה לְמִרְמָס כְּטִיט חוּצוֹת ("and my enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her … my eyes shall look upon her; now shall she be trodden down like the mire of the streets"). And the like of this is much.

The fourth [answer]: the saints abhorred death lest the enemies, the unbelievers, and those who oppose the religion should find a way to the impugning of it [the religion] and the disparagement [of it], and of the existence of the Creator (mighty and exalted) — by saying: "had these [people] a just, true Creator, as they claim, He would not have caused them to die before their enemies, who [the believers] claim oppose Him — since it is not the right of the Just One to cause His saint to die and to leave His enemy [alive]." And that is the like of the saying of משה (Moses, upon him be mercy) [Exod 32:12] לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ מִצְרַיִם לֵאמֹר ("why should the Egyptians say …"), and likewise his saying thus [Deut 9:28] פֶּן יֹאמְרוּ הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתָנוּ מִשָּׁם מִבְּלִי יְכֹלֶת יי ("lest [the inhabitants of] the land from which You brought us out say, 'because the Lord was not able …'") — so he reported that, were He to destroy the nation, it would not be safe from the Egyptians' ascribing to Him that He only did that out of His inability to bring them into the land. And the like of that is the saying of דוד (David) [Ps 115:1] לֹא לָנוּ יי לֹא לָנוּ כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד ("not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to Your name give glory") — [and] He answers [Ps 115:2] לָמָה יֹּאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם וגו' ("why should the nations say …?"); and likewise the saying of אסף (Asaph) [Ps 79:10] לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם אַיֵּה נָא אֱלֹהֵיהֶם יִוָּדַע בַּגּוֹיִם לְעֵינֵינוּ ("why should the nations say, 'where now is their God?' let it be known among the nations in our sight"); and likewise the saying of יואל (Joel) [Joel 2:17] בֵּין הָאוּלָם וְלַמִּזְבֵּחַ יִבְכּוּ הַכֹּהֲנִים מְשָׁרְתֵי יי ("between the porch and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep"), and he says [Joel 2:17] לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ בָעַמִּים וגו' ("why should they say among the peoples …?"). So these are four answers in this matter; upon none of them is there reproach (laʿn), but all of them fall within the category of the warranted (bāb al-wājib).

: The fourth answer: the saints clung to life lest their premature death give God's enemies an occasion to blaspheme — to argue that a just God would not let His servant die before His foes, or that He was unable to deliver them. The prooftexts are the classic "lest the nations say" (lāmmah yoʾmeru) verses: Moses' intercessions (Exod 32:12; Deut 9:28), David (Ps 115:1-2), Asaph (Ps 79:10), Joel (Joel 2:17). Q's closing formula — none of the four answers carries laʿn (blame/reproach), all fall in bāb al-wājib (the category of the warranted/obligatory) — certifies that the saints' recoil from death is not a defect of faith but a defensible, even meritorious, motive. The Ezek 28:17 / Mic 7:10 / Prov 29:16 verses at the head of §10 actually complete the third answer (vindication over enemies); the §10 marker falls a clause later, at "the fourth answer."
§11 — Reason and waking experience show the soul feels pleasure and pain without the body

And since what we have said is established, the soul of the human being, after his death, must inevitably be in the spiritual requital (al-jazāʾ al-rūḥānī) until it is raised in its bodies. Now, a people have denied that the soul can take pleasure or feel pain without being in the body, since the pleasures that reach it reach the body first and then arrive at it from the body. So these — if they deny that [only] from the standpoint of observation (al-mushāhada) — must likewise deny also that the soul persists once it has separated from the body, since they did not observe that [either]; yet the rational and the scriptural proofs have been established for its persistence after its separation from it. And since the soul's persistence after the body has been established — even though that was not observed — it is also not to be denied that it takes pleasure and feels pain without the body, even though that was not observed.

Moreover, we have [in fact] observed the soul to be reached by pleasure and pain without that reaching the body: for there come upon the human being many matters by which his soul takes pleasure and feels pain without the body's taking pleasure or feeling pain. That is the like of the thoughts (al-khawāṭir) that occur to the human being, so that he rejoices at some of them and grieves at others; and the like of hope and expectation, at which he rejoices, so that his soul takes pleasure in it apart from his body; and likewise fear and dread, by which the soul feels pain apart from his body; and the likes of that — such as the kingship (or possession, al-mulk) in which the soul rejoices, and the loss of that, which pains the soul apart from the body. So we have observed the soul taking pleasure and feeling pain without the body's conveying that to it, and without anything of that befalling the body either.

: §11 begins the constructive demonstration that the interim spiritual requital (§1) is intelligible: the soul can experience pleasure/pain without the body. First, a tu quoque from mushāhada (observation): the deniers cannot consistently demand empirical observation for soul-without-body pleasure while accepting (on rational and scriptural grounds) soul-without-body persistence, which is equally unobserved. Second, a positive argument from waking emotion: thoughts (khawāṭir), hope, fear, the joy of possession and the pain of its loss are all felt in the soul without bodily mediation — proof that pleasure/pain are not essentially bodily. This is the psychological substructure for the eschatology of the interim state.
§12 — Dreaming proves the soul feels pleasure and pain when the bodily senses are wholly inactive

And if a sayer says: all of that reaches it and inheres in it [only] while it is in the body; but as for when it separates from the body, it is not admissible that it take pleasure or feel pain — we say: has not pleasure and pain [already] inhered in it without the body's conveying that to it, and without the body having any agency in it? So likewise it is admissible that [pleasure and pain] inhere in it while it is separated from the body. And again, we [also] observe it taking pleasure and feeling pain while it is stripped of the acts of the body and the senses (al-ḥawāss) — and that is in the state of sleep, in which the body and the senses have no agency at all. For the human being, while asleep, has had all the acts of his senses suspended; yet he may see in his sleep things he abhors, so that his soul feels a severe pain by that, and he remains thus until he wakes, whereupon that pain departs from him; and likewise he sees the thing he loves, so that his soul is gladdened by that and takes pleasure in it, until he wakes, whereupon that gladness departs from him. So we have seen the soul take pleasure and feel pain while it is stripped of the acts of the senses. And since that is so, it is admissible that it take pleasure and feel pain while it is separated from the body altogether.

: §12 closes the demonstration with the dream argument, the strongest case: in sleep the bodily ḥawāss (senses) are wholly inactive (lā fiʿl la-hā battatan), yet the dreaming soul feels real pain at frightful dreams and real pleasure at pleasant ones. Since pleasure/pain occur with the senses entirely suspended, they can occur with the body altogether absent — securing the intelligibility of the disembodied interim requital. The dream-argument for the soul's independent affectivity is a kalām and Neoplatonic commonplace; Q uses it strictly to ground the post-mortem jazāʾ rūḥānī, not a general theory of the soul.
§13 — Some colleagues: the interim pleasure/pain is the soul's foreknowledge of its coming reward or punishment

And some of our colleagues (baʿḍ aṣḥābinā) said that the pleasure that befalls the soul of the righteous one, after its separation from the body, until the time of [full] reward, is that it knows that it is passing to the reward — so it is gladdened by that; and that is like one who is promised that, after a time, he will be rewarded with gifts and robed [in a robe of honor]: he is gladdened by that promise before he attains those gifts and that robe. Likewise the gladness is the pleasure of the soul in that state, until it passes to the reward. And likewise what befalls the soul of the disobedient one of pain is that it knows it is passing to the punishment — so it is grieved by that until it passes to it; and that grief is the pain of the soul, like one who is threatened that he will be beaten with the whip or killed: he is in a pain of grief until he passes to that beating and killing.

: §13 records a particular view of "some of our colleagues" (baʿḍ aṣḥābinā — fellow Karaite mutakallimūn) identifying the content of the interim spiritual requital: it is anticipatory — the righteous soul's joyful foreknowledge of its coming reward, the wicked soul's anxious foreknowledge of its coming punishment. The two homely analogies (the man gladdened by a promised robe-of-honor before receiving it; the man tormented by a threatened flogging before it falls) make the interim state a real but proleptic affect, fully consistent with the deferral of complete recompense to the separate abode (§2). Q reports this without explicitly endorsing it, as he reports the parallel two-views structure elsewhere (cf. Bab 10 §33).
§14 — Equal deserts require equal recompense, so requital cannot follow immediately upon each death

And among what adds to the indication that the reward and the punishment are not immediately upon death is what has been established of their being eternalized (taʾbīd). That is, [consider] two souls equal in obedience: it inevitably follows that they must be equal in reward. Yet if one of them was [received] before the other by a thousand years, or by thousands of years, and then each one of them came to be in the reward immediately upon his death — then [one] would have attained, of the reward, a surplus over the other of thousands of years — and that is not admissible. And likewise if they were equal in disobedience and there were between them this long span: [one] of them would have attained, of the punishment, the surplus of a long span. So it follows from that that the coming-to-be of mankind in the reward and the punishment is [all] together, with no precedence and no delay.

: The capstone argument, and the bab's tightest: since reward and punishment are eternal (muʾabbad — the doctrine established in Bab 9), administering them immediately at each death would make two equally-deserving souls unequally rewarded — the earlier-dying righteous soul would enjoy an infinite-bearing head start of "thousands of years" of bliss over an equally-righteous later one (and symmetrically for the damned). Justice (istiḥqāq-proportionality) therefore requires that requital befall all mankind simultaneously — "with no precedence and no delay" — at the single Day of Requital, exactly the separate-abode thesis of §2. This is why an interim (non-final, anticipatory) jazāʾ rūḥānī is needed for the intervening period — closing the circle back to §1. The argument is the temporal/quantitative complement to the spatial "distinct abodes" argument of §2.

- The bab's subject and the bare heading. The heading is only fī dhālika ("on that") — Q's signal that Bab 11 continues, without a fresh topic-statement, the eschatological discussion of the immediately preceding babs. The supplied title above reads the subject off the body: the interim state of the soul between death and the bodily resurrection (treated in Bab 8), and the doctrine that complete reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-tāmm al-ṣarf) are deferred to a single separate abode and a simultaneous Day of Requital. The bab thus sits between Bab 8 (the resurrection of the body) and Bab 12 (the Reckoning, al-ḥisāb) within the thawāb / ʿiqāb block (glossary §VI).

- The two-abodes / simultaneity architecture. Q's controlling thesis is delivered in two complementary arguments that bracket the bab: the spatial argument (§2) — God has fixed non-overlapping "ranks and bounds," this world being exclusively the dār al-taklīf wa-l-ʿamal and requital belonging to a separate abode — and the temporal argument (§14) — eternal recompense administered at each individual death would unjustly advantage the earlier-dying among equally-deserving souls, so requital must be simultaneous for all. Between them sits the need for an interim requital (§1, §13), since the soul cannot be left muhmala (idle, deprived of its deserts) in the meantime.

- The four-answers set-piece (§§7-10). The objection (§3) — if death is good, why did the saints dread it? — is met not with one reply but with a formally enumerated four: (1) the soul's natural attachment to companions and to immediate pleasure; (2) the wish to accrue more reward through longer obedience; (3) the wish to witness vindication over enemies and to deny them the shamāta of outliving the righteous; (4) the wish to deny God's enemies an occasion to blaspheme. Q's closing certification — none carries laʿn (blame), all fall in bāb al-wājib — is doctrinally pointed: the saints' recoil is not weak faith but warranted. Note that the section-markers fall a clause after the natural sense-breaks (the §10 marker lands mid-way through the enemies-material that completes the third answer); the markers have been mirrored exactly as Nemoy's Arabic places them, with the sense-flow noted in the footnotes.

- The accommodation theory of the long-life promise (§6). A genuinely interesting move: the Torah's promise of longevity to the obedient seems to undercut the claim that the deferred otherworldly reward is superior (why promise the lesser good?). Q's answer — the soul is maṭbūʿ on loving al-khayr al-muʿajjal, the immediate good, so God accommodates the promise to human psychology and thereby binds the ḥujja doubly — turns a potential embarrassment into a theory of pedagogical revelation, illustrated by the Exodus generation's craving for immediate relief after slavery.

- The soul-without-body affectivity argument (§§11-12). To make the interim jazāʾ rūḥānī intelligible, Q argues the soul feels pleasure/pain without bodily mediation, by three steps: a tu quoque on mushāhada (you accept unobserved soul-persistence, so do not demand observation here), an argument from waking emotion (hope, fear, the joy of possession are felt in the soul, not the body), and the decisive argument from dreaming (in sleep the senses are wholly inactive, yet the soul feels real pleasure and pain). This is a compact philosophical psychology marshalled for a strictly eschatological purpose.

This bab is exceptionally citation-dense — it strings together perhaps fifty biblical verses, mostly Davidic Psalms, often as bare incipits with marginal pointers. The re-OCR diff-report logs 257 Hebrew disagreements between the Kraken and multimodal passes; the multimodal Hebrew (used in the merged source) is markedly cleaner but the marginal verse-pointers remain heavily corrupted, and in several places Q's own source mis-points or transposes a reference. Where Q's quoted Hebrew makes the referent certain, the bracketed reference has been corrected to standard versification; one substantive anomaly is flagged at (a Job verse cited under Jeremiah's name) and another at (a conflated Hab 1:12 / Isa 38:19 quotation). No Arabic-prose lacunae of consequence remain; the prose is continuous across both files.
